sections.h2: What should I know before selling a house in Atlantic City?
sections.html:
Selling in Atlantic City means dealing with a barrier-island city of about 11 square miles of land where casino tourism, flood maps and a renter-heavy housing stock all affect what a buyer will pay and how fast a deal can close. Your three realistic paths are a traditional listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale, or an as-is cash purchase.

Whichever you pick, the same local paperwork applies: a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate, any city occupancy or landlord filings tied to the property, and a deed recorded with Atlantic County. The sections below walk through each piece and point to the city or county office that handles it.

sections.h2: How big is Atlantic City and what do local housing numbers look like?
sections.html:
Atlantic City had an estimated 38,787 residents in mid-2025, up slightly from 38,497 counted in the 2020 census, and it covers 10.76 square miles of land. Only 30.3% of homes are lived in by their owners, which means rentals make up most of the housing stock.

Those figures describe the whole city, from Ducktown to the Marina District, so a house near the Boardwalk and one in an inland block can sit far apart on price. Ask for recent sold prices on your own street instead of relying on a citywide median.

sections.h2: How does the casino economy shape home sales on Absecon Island?
sections.html:
Casinos set the rhythm of the local economy, and that carries into housing demand. New Jersey voters approved casino gambling in Atlantic City in 1976, and the first casino opened in 1978. The census shows accommodation and food service sales of about $3.79 billion for 2022, the largest line in the city's business totals.

Gross gaming revenue for the nine operating casinos reached $2.79 billion in 2022, as reported on Wikipedia. Four casinos closed in 2014, and Wikipedia also notes that the Atlantic City area had the highest foreclosure rate in the nation in 2019. Expect buyers to ask detailed questions about condition, flood status and rent rolls.

  • Tourism district areas named in state planning include the Marina District, Ducktown, Chelsea, South Inlet, Bader Field and Gardner's Basin.
  • The Boardwalk runs about 4 miles inside city limits, with casino hotels along it.
  • AtlantiCare Regional Medical Center, founded in 1898, runs its Atlantic City campus in town.

sections.h2: Do flood maps affect selling a house in Atlantic City?
sections.html:
Yes, because the whole city sits on a barrier island and buyers and lenders look at flood zone status early. Superstorm Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, caused flooding and power outages, and destroyed the northern boardwalk section fronting Absecon Inlet in the South Inlet neighborhood.

The city's website carries a Property Flood Information page, a Flood Insurance Rate Map, links to the FEMA flood map viewer and a floodplain development form. Before you list, look up your lot's flood zone and pull any elevation certificate you have, since a buyer's insurance quote can change their offer.

sections.h2: What inspections and certificates does Atlantic City require?
sections.html:
Atlantic City's Licensing and Inspection division runs occupancy inspections, and its Fire Prevention forms include a Smoke Detector Application and a Smoke Certificate Affidavit. Call the division before you list so you know which certificate your sale needs.

The city publishes a checklist for the certificate of occupancy on a residential rental unit. Inspectors look at both outside and inside conditions, and the list is a useful pre-sale walkthrough even for an owner-occupied house.

  • Outside: trip hazards in curbs and sidewalks, house number, siding, gutters, windows, railings, roof, fence, steps, foundation and high grass.
  • Inside: working deadbolt, smoke detectors on each level within 10 feet of sleeping areas, a 2A10BC fire extinguisher, carbon monoxide detection, GFCI outlets in bathrooms, two outlets per bedroom, working appliances and no leaks.
  • Seasonal items: window screens from May 1 to October 1 and heat at 68 degrees from October 1 to May 1.
  • Utilities must be on and the unit clean at the time of inspection.

sections.h2: What if the house is a rental or short-term rental?
sections.html:
You will need to deal with the city's landlord and rental rules, because Atlantic City has a Landlord Registration form, a Short Term Rental Public Form and a short-term rental complaint hotline. If tenants live in the house, confirm your registration is current before you sign a contract.

The city also lists a Lead Certification form under Licensing and Inspection, with a list of certified lead evaluation contractors. If you own a rental, ask the department whether a lead certificate is on file for your unit. Give any buyer copies of the leases so they know what they are taking over.

sections.h2: How are the deed and sale fees handled at closing?
sections.html:
The Atlantic County Clerk records the deed, and the main office is at 5901 Main Street in Mays Landing, with a satellite office at 1333 Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City. The clerk's recording page says checks for recording and realty transfer fees go to the Atlantic County Clerk's Office, while Gross Income Tax checks go to the State of NJ Division of Taxation.

New Jersey puts the realty transfer fee on the seller. For a sale of $350,000 or less, the state schedule runs $2.00 per $500 up to $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. With a citywide typical home value near $207,400, many Atlantic City deals land in that lower schedule.

Sellers who live outside New Jersey file a GIT/REP form, and the state sets a minimum prepayment of 2% of the consideration shown in the deed. Your closing agent usually handles those filings.

sections.h2: Should I list, sell it myself, or take a cash offer in Atlantic City?
sections.html:
The right choice depends on condition, timing and how much work you want to do before closing. A listing can reach more buyers but usually means repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal and inspection timeline.

A cash buyer purchasing as-is can skip the repair list, though the city certificate, deed recording and fee steps above still apply. If foreclosure, back taxes or a tenant problem is driving the sale, compare the written terms of every option, including who pays the transfer fee and whether any certificate work falls on you. The city's website also lists a First Time Homebuyer Program, which can matter if your likely buyer is a local household.

faqs.q: Does Atlantic City require an inspection before I sell?
faqs.a: Ask Licensing and Inspection before listing, since the city issues occupancy permits and runs the smoke certificate process through Fire Prevention. Its published checklist covers smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, outlets, heat and exterior condition, so fixing those items in advance avoids delays.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee on an Atlantic City sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The state sets the rate per $500 of consideration, and the county clerk collects it when the deed is recorded in Atlantic County.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed for an Atlantic City house?
faqs.a: Deeds go to the Atlantic County Clerk, whose main recording office is on Main Street in Mays Landing. A satellite office operates on Atlantic Avenue in Atlantic City.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Atlantic City house that has tenants or short-term guests?
faqs.a: Yes. Keep landlord registration and any short-term rental paperwork current, and hand the buyer the lease terms. The city has registration forms and a complaint hotline, so open violations are worth clearing first.

faqs.q: Does flood risk change how an Atlantic City house sells?
faqs.a: It can, because the city sits on a barrier island and buyers check flood zones and insurance costs. The city website links to its flood map, FEMA tools and a property flood information page you can review before you list.
